newsitem.title: USA: Farm state congressmen see House okaying China MFN.
newsitem.headline: Farm state congressmen see House okaying China MFN.

text.p: Farm state congressmen said they were optimistic the House would vote later Tuesday to continue normal trade relations with China.

Rep. Charles Stenholm, a Texan who leads a coalition of conservative Democrats, told reporters he expected the House to approve "by a healthy majority" President Clinton's decision to again extend most-favored-nation trade status to China.

Rep. Cal Dooley, a California Democrat, said he expected more than half the House Democrats to vote for extending MFN. With expected Republican support, the final tally in favor of extending could be in the range of 240 to 250 votes, he said.
Supporters only need a simple majority, or 218 votes, to continue MFN for an additional year. Last year, the House backed MFN for China by a vote of of 286-141.
"I think the votes are there" for extending MFN, said Rep. Bill Barrett, a Nebraska Republican and chairman of the House Agriculture subcommittee on general farm commodities.

Barrett and the other lawmakers talked with reporters after Clinton administration officials briefed the House Agriculture Committee in a closed-door meeting on the importance to U.S. farm exports of maintaining MFN status for China.
"There's still a few (members of the farm panel) who haven't made up their minds as yet," Stenholm said. But it's time for those members to "fish or cut bait," he said.
Whatever message denying MFN might send to China in the short term, it would be "fatal in the long-term" to U.S. agriculture because China would turn elsewhere for its huge import needs, he said.
Paul Drazek, USDA's top trade official, offered a similar assessment for reporters after the closed-door briefing.
If the U.S. does not extend MFN, "China will simply buy their agricultural imports from our competitors. End of story," he said.
USDA currently forecasts U.S. farm exports to China in fiscal 1997 (October-September) at $2.0 billion, up from 1.83 billion in fiscal 1996.
However, the fiscal 1997 forecast is closer to $4.0 billion when trade with Hong Kong, which will soon revert to Chinese control, is included, Drazek said.
Some sticky market access issues remain in negotiations with China on its application to join the World Trade Organization, Drazek said.
Nonetheless, the U.S. has a huge agricultural trade surplus with China, as it does with most other countries, he said.
Meanwhile, a report prepared for the Congressional Research Service by the WEFA Group offered additional evidence Tuesday of importance of the Chinese market to U.S. farmers.

If the U.S. were to deny MFN and China were to retaliate by ending its purchases of U.S. commodities, the resulting drop in prices would reduce U.S. net farm income by about $1.0 billion in fiscal 1997 and about $1.7-1.8 billion in fiscal 1998 and 1999, the report said.
